I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-08-21 19:24 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-08-22T02:24:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 4.797 degrees and its azimuth is 281.419 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 21.168 degrees and its azimuth is 165.801 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 68.58 percent illuminated, 111.684 degrees from the Sun, and 402237.1 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes — very likely.

At 68.6% illuminated, the Moon is a bright waxing gibbous and is easily bright enough to see in daylight under clear skies. An altitude of about 21° puts it comfortably above the horizon, though not very high, and its azimuth of 166° means it is in the south-southeast.

The main challenge is not brightness but locating it against a blue sky. Since the Sun is low in the west (azimuth ~281°) while the Moon is far away in the south-southeast, you can look safely in the Moon’s direction without being near the Sun. Find the south-southeastern sky, about two fist-widths at arm’s length above the horizon (roughly 20°), and scan slowly for a pale, sharply edged gibbous disk.

With clear air and normal eyesight, you should be able to spot it—especially if you use a building edge, tree, or other fixed reference to steady your search.
